You get a list of whole numbers and a target. Exactly one pair of numbers in the list adds up to the target: return their two positions. You can't use the same position twice.

With prices [30, 12, 45, 8] and a budget of 53, the answer is [2, 3]: 45 and 8 make 53.

Brute Force

Try every pair: for each number, look at every number after it.

def two_sum_slow(numbers, target):
    for i in range(len(numbers)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(numbers)):
            if numbers[i] + numbers[j] == target:
                return [i, j]

It works, but with 10,000 numbers that's about 50 million pairs. The time grows with the square of the list: O(n²).

The Key Idea

When you stand on a number, you already know which number would complete it: target - number. The question becomes "have I seen that number before?", and a hash map (a Python dict) answers it in constant time on average.

So walk the list once. For each number, look up its complement in the map. If it's there, you're done. If not, remember the number and its position, and move on.

The Solution

def two_sum(numbers, target):
    seen = {}  # number -> its position
    for i, number in enumerate(numbers):
        complement = target - number
        if complement in seen:
            return [seen[complement], i]
        seen[number] = i

Step by Step

With [30, 12, 45, 8] and a target of 53:

Position Number Complement In seen? seen after
0 30 23 No {30: 0}
1 12 41 No {30: 0, 12: 1}
2 45 8 No {30: 0, 12: 1, 45: 2}
3 8 45 Yes, at 2 Return [2, 3]

Complexity

Solution Time Extra space
Double loop O(n²) O(1)
One-pass map O(n) O(n)

You trade memory for speed: the map can hold up to n numbers.

Common Mistakes

  • Storing before checking. If you put the number in the map first, a target of 10 with a 5 in the list would match the 5 with itself.
  • Sorting the list. Sorting and using two pointers also works, in O(n log n), but sorting loses the original positions, which the problem asks for.
  • Duplicates. With [4, 4] and a target of 8, the check-then-store order gives [0, 1], which is right.
